newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Chinese made to pay in zinc flutter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chinese made to pay in zinc flutter.

text.p: Chinese producers who bet millions of dollars on a fall in zinc prices in what now looks like a poorly-timed trading strategy fell foul of those who backed a rise, including a large Western merchant, funds and other speculators.

The Chinese were on Monday fighting to wrest metal for immediate delivery against their positions in the London metals market from the clutches of the small group of merchants and funds who are making them pay for their one-way punt against market forces.

A multi-million dollar loss was seen as the likely outcome of the Chinese positions although, whilst losing in the futures market, these seemed paradoxically to be increasingly profitable in physical trade.

Using firm supply-demand fundamentals as a guide, other buyers had established substantial long positions in zinc, which has become the most rapidly appreciating asset on the London Metal Exchange (LME), rising 60 percent since the start of 1997.
The Chinese smelters which produce refined zinc for sale on the LME took the opposite strategy, selling up to 250,000 tonnes of zinc at $1,100 per tonne, seen as a good price at the time.

They had intended to buy it back, cheaply, in time for delivery in September, reaping huge profits into the bargain. But instead, as zinc moved more than $500 per tonne higher, they faced losses of up to $100 million.
However, analysts said that with increased prices and higher production, China would probably recoup much of its futures loss in substantially higher revenues from the sale of physical metal.

As prices spiralled, boosted by the expectation that the Chinese would have to buy more in the international market to meet commitments, China exported 140 percent more copper in the first half of 1997.
It is uncertain how closely the Chinese have matched physical with futures, but analyst Robin Bhar of LME brokers Brandeis said that there would still be a net loss.
He added that China was now on target to produce some 500,000 tonnes of zinc, which may achieve an average price of $1,600 per tonne, a marked improvement on 1996.
The market closed at $1,671 per tonne in Monday's kerb, up $47 on the previous day. Traders said they expect zinc to rise to $1,800 in the short term.
The premium for metal for immediate delivery over that for delivery in three months time rose to over $90, and traders expect this to reach $200 as the tightness increases in August/September.

"The battle line between China National Nonferrous Metals Corp and 'Western funds' have been well and truly drawn. The Chinese promise to export huge amounts of zinc in the face of what they see as a concerted attempt by Western traders and funds to force maximum losses from their short positions," said analyst Jim Lennon at Macquarie Equities.
Other commodity markets could not match the drama in zinc although gold advanced to trade at around $327 per ounce in late London, up some $3 from Friday.
Dealers described the gain as technical, helped by fund buying.
